brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about housing?
brief.answer:
The most decision-relevant recent finding in the record is the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation’s State of the nation's housing 2022-23 report, cited by a Labor minister as confirming the need for all government, industry and housing stakeholders to work together and as showing that the proposed Housing Australia Future Fund would double the number of new social housing dwellings added to stock each year for at least the five years from 2024, compared with the period 2006 to 2021. The minister described the fund as a $10 billion fund in legislation before the parliament and insisted the government was determined to pass it, saying too many Australians, particularly vulnerable Australians, were struggling to secure safe and affordable housing.

The record also contains sharp contradictions between promises and delivery. In an earlier exchange, a minister claimed a proud housing record, pointing to a $6 billion investment in social housing that had delivered some 21,000 social housing homes and a $4.5 billion National Rental Affordability Scheme providing incentives to build 50,000 affordable rental homes. A supplementary question immediately challenged that claim, noting that only 10,671 dwellings had been allocated under the National Rental Affordability Scheme over the previous four years against a government target of 50,000 dwellings by June 2016, and asking when the remaining 35,000-plus would be delivered. Later, another minister defended the Gillard-era record by citing 14,500 social housing units complete, 80,000 premises repaired, 31,000 families benefiting, and more than 3,500 National Rental Affordability Scheme units complete out of 50,000 total, alongside 15,000 jobs for tradespeople.

The debate has shifted from stimulus-era optimism to competing crisis narratives. A 2009-era contribution described the stimulus as working, with housing finance rising 3.6 per cent in April and 13.5 per cent over the year, loans for construction of new owner-occupied homes at their highest since January 2002, and first-home buyer loans at record levels, representing 28 per cent of new loans financed. More recently, Labor speakers have described a housing crisis a generation in the making, inherited after a decade of waste and neglect, with construction costs rising at 17 per cent, the highest rate in half a century, new builds down, and coalition governments that “didn’t even bother to have a housing minister.” Coalition speakers counter that Labor has presided over a massive surge in population growth and a collapse in completions, claiming the coalition averaged 200,000 houses per year while the record is down to 170,000 after three years of Labor, and that “great, $40 billion on housing for fewer houses” than the previous government built.

The sharpest disagreements are over who blocked supply and whether announced funding was real. Labor figures accused the Greens of blocking housing supply and the Liberals of past cuts, while the Greens criticised overdevelopment and a lack of political will on urban policy, opposed projects like WestConnex, and advocated for affordable housing. One speaker accused the government of abolishing the Major Cities Unit, failing to appoint a minister for housing, issuing no national urban policy, and presenting a $75 billion infrastructure package as a sham, with only $24.3 billion actually funded and Commonwealth infrastructure grants projected to fall from 0.4 to 0.2 per cent of GDP. State Labor MPs defended their records with specific figures, including the $5.3 billion Big Housing Build with 7,600 homes completed or underway, a $1 billion regional fund, and $232.7 million in extra public housing funding to deliver 564 new homes, while pointing to Liberal governments that reduced public housing by 13,000 properties in earlier decades.

On promises versus reported outcomes, the most direct mismatches are the National Rental Affordability Scheme target compared with allocations, and the gap between the Coalition’s claim of a $75 billion infrastructure package and the $24.3 billion the speaker said was actually funded. There is also a direct personal clash recorded: “I was the housing minister and I passed these laws,” said one member; “You are the housing minister and you have delayed them.” The record repeatedly shows housing framed as a crisis requiring urgent legislative action, whether through the $10 billion Housing Australia Future Fund or state tenancy reforms, but with each side citing different baselines to claim either progress or failure.

sections.question: What have MPs said about housing affordability and home ownership?
sections.answer:
MPs across parties agree housing affordability is a serious national issue, but they sharply diverge on causes and solutions.

**Labor and crossbench critics** argue the crisis is driven by policy failures, especially tax concessions. They cite falling home ownership—from 68–70% (1971–2001) to below 50% by 2017, and a 60-year low—and note that for 25–34 year olds, ownership dropped from 60% to under 40% in 30 years. They point to investor activity and negative gearing as key drivers, with landlord tax losses growing from a $700 million profit in 1998–99 to a $7.8 billion loss in 2010–11. They criticise the government for rejecting Labor’s proposed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, and for measures like the foreign resident capital gains withholding increase (10% to 12.5%, threshold lowered from $2 million to $750,000) as inadequate. They also oppose early access to superannuation for housing as regressive and ineffective, and highlight that first-home buyers in Sydney need 40 years of savings for a deposit.

**Coalition speakers** defend the government’s record, arguing that home ownership is high—around 70%—and that affordability is best improved by keeping unemployment low, real wages rising, interest rates low, and ensuring land release and efficient construction. They reject claims of a crisis, noting that housing affordability in the 1990s and under the coalition was stronger than under Labor in the 1980s. They support lateral ideas like the Menzies Foundation concept and argue that government interference limiting land supply has driven up prices, costing 900,000 Australians the chance to own a home. They call for releasing more land, moving departments to regional centres, and reducing stamp duty.

**A crossbench MP** proposed a nuanced approach: expanding the Reserve Bank’s duty to include housing affordability, reviewing negative gearing, using superannuation for homebuyers, and introducing owner-occupier deductibility and a home hedge fund. Another criticised both major parties for abandoning evidence-based policy, proposing investor-driven inflation controls and strategic decentralisation while opposing scrapping negative gearing.

**One speaker** highlighted the role of bipartisan inquiries, noting that home ownership fell from over 70% in the early 1970s to a 60-year low, and warned that within 10 years less than 50% of Australians will own their home. They called on leaders to set aside politics and work together on spreading wealth and stabilising families through home ownership.

sections.question: What positions have been taken on negative gearing and property tax concessions?
sections.answer:
Labor’s current policy, set to start 1 July 2027, restricts negative gearing to newly built residential properties and halves the capital gains tax discount, aiming to help first-home buyers and boost housing supply. Supporters argue these concessions overwhelmingly benefit wealthier Australians—over 50% of negative gearing benefits go to the top 20% of earners—and distort investment away from productive uses. The Greens and some economists, including via a Senate motion, have backed reform, citing rising house prices from six times young income in 1990 to twelve times in 2013.

Opponents, including the Coalition and some crossbench voices, call negative gearing “income tax 101,” standard practice for over 1.4 million Australians, and warn Labor’s changes would crash property prices, destabilise rental markets, and hurt mums and dads, nurses, and teachers—not just wealthy investors. They also point to internal Labor inconsistency: the Leader of the Opposition said in 2023 that negative gearing changes were “not on our radar,” while a Labor frontbencher later claimed the policy had been 18 months in the making. The Coalition instead favours targeted measures like removing travel deductions and imposing vacancy charges on foreign-owned empty properties, while rejecting broad negative gearing or capital gains changes.

sections.question: What has parliament said about social and public housing supply?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate shows broad agreement that social and public housing supply is inadequate, but sharp disagreement over the cause and the solution.

Government speakers, including Minister Wong and others, argued that supply is the key driver of housing affordability and rental stress. They pointed to the $32 billion Homes for Australia plan and a target of 55,000 new social and affordable homes over five years, contrasting this with the previous coalition government's record of building only 373 social and affordable homes in nine years. A government representative also noted that over 5,000 of those 55,000 homes were already complete, with 25,000 in planning or construction.

Opposition and crossbench speakers countered that the government's delivery is far too small relative to need. One senator noted that around 190,000 households are on the public housing waitlist, while the government's plan supports at most 55,000 households over 25 years, arguing the scale of delivery does not match demand. Another speaker cited figures of 148,000 on public housing waiting lists and 40,000 on community housing waiting lists, alongside $7.6 billion in Commonwealth housing expenditure in 2016-17.

Specific state-level criticisms were also raised. Rod Roberts highlighted that in South Australia, between 2016 and 2021, the government added 2,257 social housing dwellings but disposed of 3,269, a net loss of over 1,012 dwellings, while nearly 50,000 people remained on the waiting list. Sonia Hornery cited a Compass Housing report showing 48,000 households on the New South Wales waiting list and 175,904 eligible, criticising the government's Future Directions policy for proposing fewer dwellings than half the current waiting list over a decade.

A speaker from the Barwon region urged the Minister for Housing to increase public housing supply, noting 7,101 households on the priority waitlist and that only 72 of 400 planned dwellings at the Commonwealth Games village site were for social and affordable housing. They argued the market has failed, pointing to a decline in public housing from 22% of new housing in 1956 to less than 2% now.

Other speakers called for redirecting tax concessions like negative gearing and capital gains discounts—costing billions annually—to affordable housing, citing reports from Anglicare and the Grattan Institute on rental stress and falling homeownership. One speaker supported a documents motion on planning reforms, noting the New South Wales parliamentary research service found no clear local evidence for government claims that changes would improve affordability or supply.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Housing Supply?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on housing supply has been extensive, with government speakers repeatedly framing supply as the central solution to the housing crisis. One government member stated: "action on supply is critical, and more supply means better affordability. That's what we're delivering, and an Albanese Labor government is building Australia's future. That is what we will keep fighting for—more homes more quickly in more parts of the country." Another said: "We have a plan that is focused on supply, because that is the key, whether you want to be a homeowner, or you are a renter or someone in social and affordable housing. That's why our $32 billion Homes for Australia plan is worthy of the support of everyone in this parliament." A minister also claimed the budget is "a pro-supply budget," arguing that "as a whole we will see an increase in the supply of housing over the next decade if you look at all of the budget measures," including "an extra 75,000 first home buyers."

Opposition figures challenged the government's record. Senator Bragg argued that "the proposition that is facing the Australian people is really one of a lack of housing supply. Until the government is able to better understand what is holding back the supply, by talking to builders, developers and tradespeople, then they will never solve this crisis." He also criticised the government's tax changes, claiming "its own budget papers, its own word, confirm that these measures will decrease supply." Another opposition member said the government's 1.2 million homes target by 2029 is "a program that we know from Treasury is already very unlikely. In fact, from their assessment, it won't be met," adding that "supply is part of the answer, but ignoring the question of demand is a red flag."

Government speakers also blamed the coalition for past inaction. One said: "the coalition were in government for 10 years, and, for those 10 years, they neglected housing. You can't turn around the supply of housing in a year or even one term." Another accused Senator Bragg and the Australian Greens of having "blocked housing supply" for so long. In committee estimates, a departmental official noted that the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council's modelling, in its *State of the housing system 2025* report, suggests Australia "will be in a housing supply deficit at the end of the Housing Accord period" under baseline population growth, and only in surplus if population growth is 15 per cent less. The record also includes a claim that One Nation and the coalition "voted to delay the government's Help to Buy housing scheme bill, stalling a key initiative to support housing affordability."

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Environmental Planning and Assessment Amendment (Planning System Reforms) Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
The New South Wales Parliament debated the Environmental Planning and Assessment Amendment (Planning System Reforms) Bill 2025 extensively, with the Government and Opposition supporting it and The Greens opposing it. Minister Paul Scully reported an "almost universally positive response" to the bill's passage, citing praise from the Planning Institute of Australia, the Master Builders Association, and Local Government NSW, and noting the Opposition "welcomed the passage" and conceded "the reform should have been done years ago." Labor MPs like Maryanne Stuart (Heathcote), Edmond Atalla (Mount Druitt), Clayton Barr (Cessnock), and David Mehan (The Entrance) spoke in support, arguing it modernises a system from 1979, streamlines approvals, and boosts housing supply. Opposition MP Richie Williamson (Clarence) said he "broadly support[s]" the bill, calling it important for getting "more homes built without adding cost or complexity," while noting regional councils' nervousness.

The Greens strongly opposed the bill. Sue Higginson, Kobi Shetty (Balmain), and Amanda Cohn argued it "centralises power," creates "significant corruption risk," weakens environmental protections, and reduces community participation. Higginson claimed ICAC "was not asked to comment on the bill" and that the Minister's consultation claims were "misleading," while Shetty called it "a gift for developers" that will not fix affordability. Cohn quoted the Premier as saying of local government, "we've been rolling over the top of them for the last two years, and now we're about to formalise it with the bill." The Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party's Mark Banasiak expressed concerns about fast-tracking mines and renewable projects, while the Libertarian Party's John Ruddick supported the bill as "supply-side economics" and "a good step in the right direction." Minister Penny Sharpe, replying in the Legislative Council, defended the bill as addressing a housing crisis and legal uncertainties, and noted the Government would support an Opposition amendment on local strategic planning oversight.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Energy policy and housing?
sections.answer:
Several speakers addressed both energy policy and housing, often linking them. A government minister (Commonwealth) said the coalition is "completely out of touch, not just with energy policy but also with the housing experience of Australians," citing former leaders Malcolm Turnbull and Joe Hockey as evidence. The same minister stated housing is "an absolutely foremost priority of our government in this second term" and that "Housing is in crisis in our country." Another government speaker accused the coalition of being "housing hypocrites" and claimed they are "busy fighting culture wars against non-existent enemies," while a coalition speaker countered that Labor "legislates ambition without resourcing it" in housing, citing the 1.2 million homes commitment, and said of Labor's "energy policy of 82 per cent renewables—ain't gonna happen!"

On the substance of energy and housing policy, the Hon. Bob Nanva (New South Wales) said the NSW Government "is not supportive of banning new gas connections, because households should have choice," while detailing decarbonisation efforts: the Energy Savings Scheme, the Consumer Energy Strategy, 35 per cent renewable energy, and EV charging rollout figures. He noted NSW "became the first State to mandate seven‑star thermal performance for all new homes" in 2023, projecting savings of approximately $1,070 per year on energy bills. In contrast, Ms Abigail Boyd (New South Wales) moved a motion congratulating the Victorian Government, the ACT Government and various NSW councils for mandating electrification, and called on the government to "ban new gas connections for residential and commercial developments." She cited the Net Zero Commission's 2024 report finding NSW "is not on track to meet emission reduction targets" and that the built environment sector "nearly doubled greenhouse gas emissions between 2005 and 2022," and quoted the Property Council supporting the City of Sydney's electrification mandate.

A Western Australian speaker (Commonwealth) praised that state's approach: "Our domestic gas reservation policy has protected us from some of the worst volatility that has been seen on the east coast," and claimed that under the coalition "household electricity prices rose by nearly 20 per cent." Senator Gallagher (Commonwealth, at estimates) said the government is "working across government" on housing, energy and regulatory reduction, but that the coalition votes against reform bills "and then you come in here and complain." The record also includes a coalition speaker claiming the government "had 23 different energy policies over that period" and is "divided, confused and uncertain," while another government speaker quoted the shadow minister for housing as saying, "We've been too busy talking about the internals of the Liberal Party to do any work."

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Strata Schemes Legislation Amendment Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on the Strata Schemes Legislation Amendment Bill 2024 shows it was a New South Wales Government bill implementing 37 recommendations from the 2021 statutory review of strata laws, with Labor members describing it as the second tranche of reforms. Labor's Julia Finn (Granville) said the bill aims to "improve the management and governance of strata schemes," enhancing "transparency, accountability and the overall functioning" of the more than 86,000 schemes in the state. Labor's Edmond Atalla (Mount Druitt) said it would "strengthen accountability to ensure trust in strata managing agents and building managers," prohibit unfair contract terms, improve committee governance, and tackle noncompliance in maintaining common property. Labor's Jodie Harrison (Charlestown) said it would make strata living "fairer for the 1.2 million people living in the 86,000 schemes" and help owners in financial hardship by requiring levy notices to include information on payment options and financial counselling.

Labor's Greg Warren (Campbelltown) said the bill would "uplift developer and strata managing agent professionalism," require owners' corporations to maintain common property, and assist owners in financial hardship, including by increasing the notice of debt recovery action from 21 days to 30 days. Labor's Charishma Kaliyanda (Liverpool) highlighted reforms to strata managing agents and building managers, including prohibiting management agreements that limit agent liability, requiring six-monthly activity reports, and imposing a statutory obligation for building managers to act in the owners' corporation's best interests. Labor's Maryanne Stuart (Heathcote) said constituents had raised concerns about agents "misusing their authority," and that the bill would protect owners' corporations from unfair contract terms and hold developers to account. Labor's Kylie Wilkinson (East Hills) focused on reforms around environmental sustainability, financial viability and accessibility, including prohibiting by-laws that block sustainability infrastructure due to appearance and lowering voting thresholds for accessibility infrastructure.

Minister Anoulack Chanthivong (Macquarie Fields), in reply, said the bill was "the most significant reforms to strata living and strata laws since 2015," and that the Government had implemented 31 recommendations in December 2023, passed the Strata Managing Agents Legislation Amendment Act 2024 in September 2024, and was progressing the remaining 36 legislative recommendations. Minister Jihad Dib (Bankstown) said the bill made changes to conveyancing laws to improve disclosure of embedded networks as part of the sale of a lot, including new disclosure requirements for "exclusive supply networks." Labor's Stephanie Di Pasqua (Drummoyne) said the bill would "go some way to improving the many issues that are experienced by owners in strata schemes," while noting "there is always more work to be done."

sections.question: What have MPs said about housing affordability and home ownership since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several MPs addressed housing affordability and home ownership. In the New South Wales Parliament, Ms Jenny Leong (The Greens) said the Help to Buy shared equity scheme would assist an estimated 3,000 first home buyers per year in NSW, or 12.9 per cent of the over 23,000 who bought their first home in the 12 months to July 2024. She argued demand-side subsidies like this are "inflationary" and "push up the cost of housing", citing evidence from the Senate inquiry that the money "is eventually capitalised into house prices, so the beneficiaries gain at the expense of everyone else". She said the scheme is "good for the 40,000 lucky recipients of it and worse for everybody else" and asked what the Government will do for the remaining 87 per cent of first home buyers.

Mr Stephen Bali (Labor, NSW) supported the bill, saying home ownership for low to middle income households is getting more difficult in Sydney. He noted the scheme modernises a 1980s shared equity program that helped people "participate in the housing market rather than simply pay rent". He cited the Grattan Institute's prediction that the scheme will increase house prices by just 0.016 per cent, or $160 per $1 million spent on a home. Ms Eleni Petinos (Liberal, NSW Opposition) also supported the bill but criticised the Minns Labor Government for closing the NSW Shared Equity Home Buyer scheme on 30 June 2024, just seven months after opening it to domestic violence victims, and for cutting support for anyone buying a home worth over $1 million.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a Labor MP said the Albanese government is implementing a "$43 billion agenda" on housing, having taken the Commonwealth "from being, really, a negligent bystander" to "the boldest and most ambitious Australian government on housing since the Second World War". Another Labor MP said the government inherited a "housing horror show" in May 2022, with building costs rising at 17 per cent, and criticised the coalition for a "decade of waste and neglect" and for not even having a housing minister. A Commonwealth MP also noted that house prices have risen by 400 per cent over two decades, ownership is down by seven per cent for young people, and just 44 per cent of Australians aged 25 to 34 own a home.

sections.question: What positions have been taken on negative gearing and property tax concessions since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Government speakers—including Senator Gallagher and other Labor members in the Commonwealth Parliament—have defended reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax (CGT) as a way to level the playing field for first home buyers and direct investment toward new housing supply. They state that, from 1 July 2027, negative gearing for residential property purchased after budget night (7:30 pm on 12 May 2026) will be limited to new builds, with existing investments grandfathered so current owners can continue under old rules until sale. They also say the 50 per cent CGT discount will be replaced with cost-base indexation for gains accrued after 1 July 2027, plus a 30 per cent minimum tax on realised gains. One Labor speaker claims these changes are expected to help an additional 75,000 Australians buy a home over the next decade, and another says the reforms are "careful, responsible policy design" that protects existing investment decisions.

Opposition and crossbench speakers have taken contrary positions. A coalition speaker criticises the reforms as attacking negative gearing and gutting CGT concessions "while doing nothing about bracket creep," and claims the changes will "cripple nearly 300,000 small businesses" that use trusts, calling those affected "battlers; they're not billionaires." A Greens speaker alleges Labor has "wasted $53 billion on tax concessions for wealthy property investors" over four years and, citing PBO analysis, says further delay would waste another $190 billion over the next decade, urging that revenue instead fund public and affordable housing. The same speaker calls housing affordability "a political choice." A coalition senator also moved a motion in the Economics Legislation Committee on 4 June 2026 seeking Treasury advice on the impact of housing tax changes on supply and rents.

The record also includes a Labor speaker rebutting opposition claims, saying "We are not abolishing it; we're changing it," and another noting the government will remove ministerial discretion over definitions of eligible new builds and exempt housing types, moving full definitions into primary law after consultation. A separate Labor speaker welcomes the reforms as "ambitious" and notes exemptions for new houses to incentivise supply, while a coalition speaker characterises Labor as prioritising "wealthy property investors, multiple-property owners, over regular mortgage holders and renters."

sections.question: What has parliament said about social and public housing supply since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several speakers addressed social and public housing supply. In the New South Wales Parliament, Minister for Housing Rose Jackson (Labor) reported that in 2023-24, the first year of the Minns Labor Government, 849 new public homes were completed—"the largest number of homes delivered over the past decade"—and that the state was on track to match that figure in the current year. She contrasted this with the previous government's record, noting that under that government over $3.6 billion of public housing was sold, and completions dropped to only 194 homes in 2019-20. She also stated that the turnaround time for vacant public homes had been reduced from 34.7 days in 2022-23 to 27.6 days, giving New South Wales "the fastest turnaround time for vacant homes in the country." In a separate answer, she said the government was on track to deliver 749 homes in regional New South Wales in 2025-26, up from 416 in 2023-24 and 466 the following year.

Also in the New South Wales Parliament, Stephen Lawrence (Labor) supported the Housing Amendment Bill 2025, which he said enables the delivery of the state government's commitment to build 8,400 new social homes and 21,000 new affordable and market homes under the Building Homes for NSW program. He noted the state was on track to deliver 850 new social homes in year one of that program and that the bill unlocks $4 billion of investment committed in the 2024-25 budget for Homes NSW. In the Commonwealth Parliament, a government speaker claimed that Labor's $43 billion Homes for Australia plan was delivering 5,000 social and affordable houses, with projects already underway in Tasmania, and that the Housing Australia Future Fund alone was delivering more than 600 new social and affordable homes in that state.

However, the record also contains criticism of the scale of delivery. In a Commonwealth estimates hearing on 12 February 2026, a questioner noted that social housing is "at record lows" and the public housing waitlist "at record highs," with around 190,000 households waiting, and argued that the government's plan to support at most 55,000 households in new social and affordable homes over 25 years "does not match the scale of demand." Separately, in a Commonwealth estimates hearing on 4 December 2025, a speaker acknowledged that "there's a lot of social housing stock that needs repair" but said the government through its program "has created additional supply of public and social housing that is very important for the system." The record is otherwise limited on this specific topic.

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 1993 and 2009?
eras.answer:
Parliamentary debate on housing between 1993 and 2009 was sharply partisan, spanning public housing funding, tax treatment, affordability and Indigenous housing. Labor speakers repeatedly attacked Coalition cuts to public housing. One Labor senator noted that tax expenditures on negative gearing exceeded Commonwealth-State Housing Agreement (CSHA) spending, and that rent assistance cost more than the CSHA, citing the Industry Commission's 1993 finding that public housing was more cost-effective than poorly targeted rent assistance. The same speaker said CSHA dwelling units fell from 372,134 in 1996 to 345,000 in 2003-04, and new people assisted fell from 50,000 in 1996 to 25,000, projected to drop to 15,000 by 2009. Another Labor MP said CSHA funding had been cut by $100 million plus a further $360 million, and that 250,000 households were on public housing waiting lists. A Victorian Labor MP said the Howard government cut $200 million from public housing in 1997-98, Victorian allocations fell from $242,966 to $217,565, and waiting lists in Victoria jumped from 30,076 to 53,379 between 1987 and 1997.

Government speakers defended their record. One Coalition MP argued low interest rates were the key to affordability—6.55 per cent at the time versus 10.5 per cent in 1996 and 17 per cent in the late 1980s—and touted the First Home Owners Scheme, which had helped 387,000 Australians. He said the Commonwealth contributed $4 billion over four years to the CSHA versus $1.4 billion from the states, plus $1.8 billion for rent assistance, and argued rent assistance did not lock low-income people into location-specific job markets as public housing did. A later government speaker announced a residential housing boost from 2008-09: first home buyers of new homes would receive $21,000 and buyers of existing homes $14,000.

A major recurring fight concerned the GST on permanent residents of caravan parks and boarding houses. Labor speakers said the government had promised rent would be GST-free, then applied a concessional rate that effectively meant "half of 10 becomes 5.5." They argued the $33 million rent assistance rescue package reached almost none of the 161,000 permanent caravan park residents—only 3,955 received any increase—and that threshold changes actually reduced assistance for some couples. One Labor MP quoted a constituent, Joan Armstrong of the electorate of Richmond, whose rent assistance fell by $1.50 per fortnight after a threshold rise, and accused the responsible minister of ignoring residents. The same speaker said the government's own National Homeless Strategy identified families in caravans and boarding house residents as high-risk groups, yet the government made their housing less affordable.

On Indigenous housing, one speaker said a health worker told them the key to Indigenous children's health was "improve the housing," with overcrowding—"18 people living in a house"—causal to poor outcomes. Another speaker opposed the Northern Territory intervention, arguing there was no evidence linking land control to housing provision, and criticised the Rudd government for requiring 40-year leases where the previous minister had opposed 99-year leases. By 2009, senators from multiple parties praised the Senate Select Committee on Housing Affordability report as comprehensive and balanced, with one Labor senator saying it was an "immense frustration" that the national parliament had not sufficiently engaged with housing affordability, and another noting broad agreement across community, industry and union bodies that a clear national strategy was needed.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018, Housing Affordability and Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018.
eras.answer:
In the New South Wales Parliament, the Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018 drew sharp criticism from opposition and crossbench members. Labor’s Adam Searle said the bill could “exacerbate the incidence of homelessness” and that the rental bond scheme’s ministerial guidelines gave the Minister an “absolute fiat” with no parliamentary scrutiny; he proposed amendments requiring a property condition report and broader hardship discretion. Labor’s David Mehan, citing the Legislation Review Committee, said the bill “infringes on the rights and liberties of citizens,” noting social housing stock fell from 127,024 dwellings in 2011 to 123,267 in 2016 while homelessness rose. The Greens’ Justin Field opposed the bill outright, calling it “punitive” and noting a $1,400 bond would be “five times” the weekly income of a tenant on Newstart; he also criticised that guidelines were only released late. Government speakers, including Minister Pru Goward and Melanie Gibbons (Liberal), defended the bill as targeting only tenants who wilfully damage property or commit fraud, with Goward stressing “the vast majority of good, responsible and law-abiding tenants” would be unaffected.

On the separate Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018, Labor’s David Mehan called it “a tremendous disappointment,” arguing that without banning no-grounds evictions, “all the benefits afforded by this bill… fall away.” The Greens’ Jamie Parker supported parts but pushed a 10-point plan, including ending no-grounds evictions and limiting rent increases. Minister Matt Kean (Liberal) replied that the bill struck “a balance between the interests of tenants and the interests of landlords,” and criticised Labor’s delay complaints as “pure politics.” In the Commonwealth Parliament, a government bill replaced the National Affordable Housing Agreement with a new National Housing and Homelessness Agreement, with the minister noting the old agreement “completely failed” three of four benchmarks, and another bill introduced an Automatic Rent Deduction Scheme because in 2013-14 over 8,900 social housing households had more than three weeks’ rent arrears and over 2,300 people were evicted. A further Commonwealth bill imposed an annual vacancy charge on foreign owners of vacant residential property to “increase the number of houses available for Australians to live in.”

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did parliament argue about housing between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Public Housing, Affordable Housing and HomeBuilder Program.
eras.answer:
Parliamentary debate on housing between 2020 and mid-2024 was sharply partisan. Government speakers defended their records: one coalition speaker touted that "HomeBuilder, the First Home Super Saver Scheme and the Home Guarantee Scheme have helped make the dream of home ownership a reality," citing 160,000 first-home purchases in a year and a planned doubling of the Home Guarantee Scheme to 50,000 places. Another coalition speaker praised HomeBuilder for lifting detached housing sales by 31 per cent and new-home loan approvals by 20 per cent into the September quarter, supporting an industry employing up to one million people. A Labor speaker attacked the same scheme, quoting Domain headlines calling HomeBuilder "the most-complex least-equitable construction jobs program ever devised" and asking whether it should be renamed "home blunder." A Queensland Labor Treasurer reportedly wrote to federal Labor's housing minister seeking a 12-month extension of the April 30, 2024 HomeBuilder deadline.

Labor speakers criticised the coalition's record, asking "where were your housing investments in 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2016… up to May 2022?" and described a "lost decade of minimal intervention and investment in social and affordable housing." In response, they championed the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, a $10 billion fund intended to deliver 20,000 social housing properties and 10,000 affordable homes for frontline workers over five years, alongside the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council Bill and the Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023. One Labor speaker noted the Greens and Liberals were "teaming up to oppose more investment in housing," while a crossbench speaker (PENDER) said they were "pleased that the parliament will be doing more to support those who rely on affordable and social housing" despite concerns about the government's approach.

State-level debate also featured. In South Australia, a committee report recommended the Affordable Housing Initiative, a five-year public sector program from late 2020 to 2025 delivering 1,000 new affordable home ownership opportunities across metropolitan Adelaide and regional South Australia, self-funding with a projected surplus of $15.6 million against $407.3 million in expenditure. A South Australian government speaker reported the initiative was "well underway," with a 10-year housing strategy published in December, and noted the Minister for Human Services defined an affordable housing solution as one helping a customer purchase an affordable home or secure affordable rental. The record also notes that the social and affordable housing crisis "knows no geographical boundaries," affecting essential workers, families, older women and the most vulnerable nationwide.

key_moments.title: Negative gearing and capital gains tax
key_moments.speaker: Andrew Leigh
key_moments.brief: Labor argued that negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts disproportionately benefit high-income earners, reduce home ownership, and cost the budget billions, proposing to halve the capital gains tax discount to 25% for new assets from July 2017 and grandfather existing investments. The speaker also criticised the government for scrapping Labor's permanent instant asset write-off and loss carry-back measures, and for failing to progress tax reform.
key_moments.why: Negative gearing and capital gains tax, Federal, 2016

key_moments.title: COVID-19 Rental Affordability
key_moments.speaker: R.A. Simms
key_moments.brief: The motion calls on the Marshall government to extend the eviction moratorium beyond 30 June, waive all COVID-19 rental debt, and introduce permanent rent caps, noting that no rental properties in South Australia are affordable for people on JobSeeker.

key_moments.title: Home Ownership
key_moments.speaker: Adam Crouch
key_moments.brief: Premier Dominic Perrottet announced the government's first home buyer choice policy, allowing buyers to opt for an annual land tax instead of upfront stamp duty, and noted over 13,000 people had used the online calculator, with Lakemba being the top electorate of interest.

key_moments.title: Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023
key_moments.speaker: Julie Collins
key_moments.brief: The government introduced the Housing Australia Future Fund bill, a $10 billion fund with annual disbursements capped at $500 million, intended to fund 30,000 social and affordable homes in its first five years. The bill also renames the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation as Housing Australia and establishes the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council.
key_moments.why: Second reading, Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, 2023

key_moments.title: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill
key_moments.speaker: Bolton
key_moments.brief: The speaker supported the bill to refer powers for the Help to Buy scheme, which would assist 40,000 participants nationally (2,000 in Queensland) through up to 40% Commonwealth shared equity, but noted criticisms from economist John Quiggin that subsidies are undesirable, the scheme has a lottery character, and social housing should be prioritised, while arguing the scheme is too small to address the housing crisis.
key_moments.why: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill, Queensland, 2024

key_moments.title: Housing
key_moments.speaker: Will Fowles
key_moments.brief: The speaker announced a broadcast housing crisis conversation with Major Brendan Nottle, Cr Sarah McKenzie and Rob Pradolin, arguing for urgent nonpartisan action and the Housing First principle to provide stable housing as the foundation for addressing homelessness.
